podcast.body: Originally a rock band, Wild Cherry found it increasingly difficult to get work as disco gained popularity. Rob Parissi, the band's songwriter, singer, and producer, told the band they needed to start playing more dance music. The idea for the song came from audience members at a disco where they were playing, who would ask, "When are you going to play some funky music, white boy?" Parissi wrote the first two verses and the chorus before getting to the stage, and the last verse in his car on the way home, viewing himself as a "reporter" documenting their experiences. His father had advised him to remove the "white boy" part, but it ultimately became a selling point. The song became a massive hit, reaching number one on the US Billboard Hot 100 on September 18, 1976, and also topping the Billboard Hot Soul singles chart. Many people initially believed the band was African American and were surprised to see they were white when they appeared on TV shows like American Bandstand and Midnight Special, or when opening for artists like George Benson and Santana. Despite the success, Parissi stated in 1976 that the band did not want to continue playing funk or disco. The band dissolved by the end of the 1970s after failing to produce more hits. "I wrote, sang and produced, Play That Monkey Music White Bull."

This song was a major hit for Wild Cherry, though the band struggled to achieve similar success with any subsequent releases. It marked their peak commercially and contributed to their one-hit wonder status. "I mean they had a great song with play that funky music but they could never replicate that."

This song was a number one hit for Wild Cherry, which some classify as disco, but was essentially straight-up funk despite its self-consciously satirical "White Boy" lyrics. "Essentially, their 1976 number one hit played that funky music, which some classify as disco, was really straight up funk, even with the inclusion of the self-consciously satirical lyrics White Boy."
